stories.title: Dental students put Medicaid data on the map
stories.summary: Three Harvard dental students took a massive new Medicaid dataset — 227 million rows — and turned it into a free interactive map of dental care access across the U.S. Their tool, CHOMP, lets researchers and policymakers spot gaps in oral health coverage.
stories.extended_summary: When the federal government released a massive Medicaid claims dataset in February 2026, three Harvard dental students saw what others missed: a map of who can't get dental care. Clark Morgan, Kenny Liu, and Samat Borbiev dug through 227 million rows of anonymized records to build CHOMP — Claims History of Oral Healthcare Medicaid Procedures — a free interactive tool that shows dental procedures covered by Medicaid nationwide. What would normally cost researchers thousands is now public. The goal: give policymakers a clear picture of where oral health access falls short, and who's being left out.

stories.title: Hockaday Student Honored by Girl Scouts of Northeast Texas
stories.summary: Hockaday senior Kora Thomas was honored by the Girl Scouts of Northeast Texas for a Gold Award project that brought a free soccer clinic to about 100 kids at Marcus Elementary — even through severe weather. She built a model that keeps going without her.
stories.extended_summary: About 100 kids showed up for a free soccer clinic at Marcus Elementary — in severe weather, no less. The person behind it: Hockaday senior Kora Thomas, a lifelong Girl Scout who turned her Gold Award project into a sustainable program with equipment from Dick's Sporting Goods and Sam's Club, volunteer coaches, and tutorial videos she made herself. On Oct. 9 she was named a Mary Anne Cree Young Woman of Distinction. The clinic now lives on through Coaching for Change and has already inspired another student-led version.

stories.title: Need a 1960s phone booth or a fake knife? Steel City Props has Pittsburgh covered
stories.summary: Three Pittsburgh filmmakers kept hitting the same wall — no prop house in the city — so they built their own. Steel City Props now stocks 1960s phone booths, fake knives, and a horror-movie neck stump, all in service of women-led film.
stories.extended_summary: One of their prized possessions is a neck stump from a horror movie. That tells you most of what you need to know about Steel City Props, the prop house three Point Park film grads built because Pittsburgh didn't have one. Zoe Xandra, Sarah Yobbi, and Leia Devin founded Slow Drift Collective to amplify women's voices in film, then kept blowing their own money sourcing period props and costumes. So they turned the problem into a resource: phone booths, fake weapons, appliances, an entire 1980s dance party's worth of wardrobe — available to other filmmakers who need to build a world on a budget.

stories.title: Local girl gives back, looks ahead to Florida pageant
stories.summary: Ten-year-old Amariah Lodiong has logged over 245 hours of community service and founded her own nonprofit, Amariah's Amazing Grace. She's now representing North Carolina at the National American Miss Nationals pageant.
stories.extended_summary: At five years old, on a trip to Uganda, Amariah Lodiong gave away her toys to kids who had none. She hasn't really stopped since. Now 10, the North Carolina native has founded her own registered nonprofit, Amariah's Amazing Grace, and logged more than 245 hours of community service — collecting books for refugee camps, singing for nursing home residents, feeding people who are homeless. Her mother says the giving comes from somewhere deep: "This girl came out of the womb wanting to give everything she had to everybody." Next up, she's competing at the National American Miss Nationals pageant.

stories.title: Castle Dale celebrates grand opening of new community-backed all-abilities park
stories.summary: Castle Dale just opened an all-abilities park with wheelchair ramps, sensory areas, and swings every kid can use. The wild part? A young cowboy raised over $6,000 for it by hosting goat-tying events in honor of his friend Ruger, who has Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
stories.extended_summary: A kid with a love of rodeo turned goat-tying into a fundraiser for his friend — and helped build a park where every child can play. When Axel Mead heard Castle Dale was planning an all-abilities park, he thought of his friend Ruger Henrie, who has Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Axel set a $500 goal, but his goat-tying jackpot events blew past it, and every champion gave their prize money back. In total he raised over $6,000. Nineteen months after the idea was sketched on a napkin, the park opened with wheelchair-accessible ramps, sensory areas, and swings for all.

stories.title: Free Inclusive Dance class: An amazing opportunity for people with disabilities
stories.summary: Kaylee Bayes—the first wheelchair dancer on So You Think You Can Dance—taught Somerville's first Inclusive Dance class, where people of all ages and abilities danced together to 'Golden' from KPop Demon Hunters. The class is funded, fittingly, by fines from people who illegally park in handicapped spaces.
stories.extended_summary: Kaylee Bayes started dancing at three, was diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome at 21, and was told she'd never dance again. She refused that reality—and became the first wheelchair dancer on So You Think You Can Dance. Now she's teaching Somerville's first Inclusive Dance class, where in-person and Zoom dancers of all ages and abilities moved together to 'Golden' from KPop Demon Hunters. The detail that makes it even better: the class is funded by fines collected from people who illegally park in handicapped spaces. Mayor Jake Wilson showed up to thank the commission, and attendees are already hoping the class grows.

stories.title: In Nashville, Career and Technical Education Prepares Students for College and Professional Life
stories.summary: Natalie Martinez immigrated from Honduras at 9 and worked her way into AP classes, dual enrollment, and a paid clinical internship at HCA Healthcare. Nashville's career-and-technical-education model is built so students don't have to choose between college and a career.
stories.extended_summary: Natalie Martinez arrived from Honduras at nine years old, learned English, and stacked her high school schedule with AP and honors classes — then added a paid clinical internship at HCA Healthcare her senior year. She didn't have to pick between college prep and career training, because Nashville's Academies of Nashville model doesn't make students choose. Every Metro Nashville high schooler selects a career pathway — healthcare, business, engineering — and pairs hands-on coursework with dual enrollment and industry credentials. For Martinez, whose parents sacrificed everything for her future, the result is simple: 'Nothing was going to stop me from pursuing my dreams.'

stories.title: Recent College Grad Climbs Grand Teton In Suit And Tie For LinkedIn Pic, Lands Job
stories.summary: Quinn Kunz hiked the Grand Teton in a suit and tie for a LinkedIn headshot — then did it again on Idaho's highest peak because his tie was crooked. The video blew up, and he actually got a job out of it.
stories.extended_summary: Most new grads polish a headshot. Quinn Kunz climbed the Grand Teton in a full suit and tie to take his. The 13,775-foot summit shot came out with a crooked tie, so instead of Photoshopping it, he put the suit back on and summited Borah Peak, Idaho's highest point, for take two — handing resumes to stunned climbers along the way. He posted the video on LinkedIn 'just to be funny.' It blew up, and someone who saw it offered him a job. Turns out the jacket was warmer than expected, and the stunt was a better cover letter than anything he could have typed.
